verdicts.title: Archive Extracted With A Password On The Command Line
lines: title: Archive Extracted With A Password On The Command Line
unzip or 7z extracted an archive with its password given on the command
line (unzip -P, 7z -p followed by the password). A password protects an
archive's content from scanners on the way in, which is how payloads are
often delivered; an administrator unpacking an ordinary archive gives none.
- A script that unpacks a password-protected archive it was given on purpose
verdicts.reason: it alerted on every run with changed input arguments and on no ordinary activity

verdicts.title: Private Key Files Searched With Find
lines: title: Private Key Files Searched With Find
find was asked for files named like SSH private keys: id_rsa, id_dsa,
id_ecdsa, id_ed25519 or their security key variants, by -name, -iname,
-path or -regex. Someone who uses a key knows where it is; a search for
every file with such a name looks for keys to take.
- An administrator taking stock of the keys on a host
verdicts.reason: it alerted on every run with changed input arguments and on no ordinary activity

verdicts.title: Python Startup Hook File Written
lines: title: Python Startup Hook File Written
A file named usercustomize.py or sitecustomize.py was written. Python imports
these from its site folders every time it starts, so code put in one runs in
every later Python program of that account, or of every account for a
system-wide site folder. Packages rarely ship either file, and installs write
them through the package manager, so a write outside one is worth a look.
Code in a .pth file, which Python also runs at start, is not covered.
- A developer who writes a usercustomize.py or sitecustomize.py on purpose
verdicts.reason: it alerted on every run with changed input arguments and on no ordinary activity

verdicts.title: Setuid Or Setgid Bit Set With Chmod
lines: title: Setuid Or Setgid Bit Set With Chmod
chmod set the setuid or setgid bit on a file. A program with that bit runs
with its owner's or group's rights, so setting it on a file one controls is a
way to keep or raise rights. Packages set these bits when they install, not
through chmod. The rule matches a symbolic mode that adds or sets s (u+s,
g+xs, +s, a=rwxs, a part of u+x,g+s) and a numeric mode of four digits, or
five with a leading 0, whose first digit sets either bit (4755, 2711, 04700).
- An administrator installing a setuid program by hand
verdicts.reason: it alerted on every run with changed input arguments and on no ordinary activity

verdicts.title: Shell History File Emptied
lines: A shell history file was truncated to nothing, replaced by a link to
/dev/null, or overwritten with /dev/null. Each keeps the file in place and
removes what it recorded, as covering tracks does. History files are named
after the shell or the program, and the name ends in history, as in
condition: (selection_truncate or selection_link or selection_copy) and selection_history
- Someone clearing their own history on purpose
verdicts.reason: it alerted on every run with changed input arguments and on no ordinary activity

verdicts.title: Shell History File Truncated In Place
lines: title: Shell History File Truncated In Place
A shell history file was opened, successfully, for a truncating write
(O_TRUNC), which empties it in place. A shell's own redirect does this
(> file, echo > file, cat /dev/null > file) and starts no program. Current
shells do not save their history that way: bash 4.4 and later (readline
7.0 and later), tcsh and busybox ash append with O_APPEND and rewrite the
file as a new one renamed over the old one, ksh93 appends and trims with
ftruncate, and zsh appends or renames a new file over it. Older bash and
zsh with HIST_SAVE_BY_COPY unset do truncate in place, and are false
positives. auditd's system call record holds the open's flags and not the
file's name, and its path record the name and not the flags, so the rule
takes the file from the audit key of the watch on history files,
shell-history in the lab's audit rules: with another key, put that key
here. Covers open, openat and creat on any architecture auditd names the
call for; not openat2, whose flags the record does not show, nor truncate
or ftruncate, nor a new file renamed over the history file, which is how
bash's history -c then history -w, sed -i and editors that save by rename
# The flags are hex: O_TRUNC is 0x200, a bit of the third digit from the right.
condition: selection_watch and (selection_openat or selection_open or selection_creat)
- bash creating a missing history file the first time it saves (O_CREAT|O_TRUNC), once per account
- bash before 4.4 trimming its history file on exit, or rewriting it (history -w, or on exit without histappend)
- zsh with HIST_SAVE_BY_COPY unset, saving its history
- Someone clearing their own history on purpose
verdicts.reason: it alerted on every run with changed input arguments and on no ordinary activity

verdicts.title: System Account Created With A Login Shell
lines: title: System Account Created With A Login Shell
useradd created a system account and gave it an interactive shell. Packages
create system accounts with nologin or false as their shell, so a system
account that can log in is one that someone means to use. The system option
is matched on its own (-r, --system) and among other one-letter options
- A service account that is meant to log in
verdicts.reason: it alerted on every run with changed input arguments and on no ordinary activity

verdicts.title: Systemd Unit File Written By A Shell
lines: title: Systemd Unit File Written By A Shell
A shell or tee created a systemd service or timer unit in a folder systemd
loads units from. Packages install their units with their package manager,
and systemctl writes overrides itself, so a unit written from a shell is a
service or timer someone made by hand, as persistence does.
- An administrator who writes a unit file by hand
verdicts.reason: it alerted on every run with changed input arguments and on no ordinary activity

notes: The rules were evaluated after the run ended, so an alert's time is the time of the event it matched.

A step starts when Sysmon records the shell that carries the test, and ends at a marker the lab runs after it. For a test that schedules something, the marker comes after the wait the list of tests sets.
Each sensor stamps its own records, so an event can be earlier than the start of its step, here by up to 2 ms (53 events).
Position 3 of the run was ordinary administration, not an attack step: what the rules said about it is under ordinary.
1 test on the list did not run: T1486 Encrypt files using ccrypt (FreeBSD/Linux) (the target has no ccencrypt, which the test needs).

The run accepted 9 of the 10 rules written in this repository. A match of a rule it did not accept is not in the recording. Not accepted: Program Named Like A System Daemon Run From A Temporary Folder (not every procedure it alerts on ran again with changed input arguments and took effect: T1036.003 Masquerading as FreeBSD or Linux crond process).
2 steps left more than 300 events. The recording keeps the first 300 of each and every event a rule matched, and the run's results.json holds them all.
